claims.text: Slight Al-content variations between alternating Al0.1CrCoFeNi-based layers trigger a clustering-to-ordering transition localized at multilayer interfaces under compressive loading.
Interfacial ordering increases the local yield strength.
Interfacial ordering impedes dislocation motion or propagation.
The proposed interfacial ordering mechanism improves resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation relative to a homogeneous coating.
The initial quenched Al0.1CrCoFeNi coating is single-phase and nominally compositionally homogeneous.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi generally has a stronger clustering tendency than ordering tendency before high-strain compression.
High-strain compression can induce a clustering-to-ordering transition in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
The compression-induced transition is characterized by increased unlike-pair correlations such as Al-Co and Al-Cr and decreased like-pair correlations such as Al-Al.
Chemically distinct multilayer interfaces cause ordering to occur preferentially at those interfaces.
A slight Al-content variation is sufficient to drive the proposed interfacial transition.
A homogeneous Al0.1CrCoFeNi coating does not benefit from the compression-induced ordering mechanism because it lacks chemically engineered interfaces.
The engineered multilayer coating will accumulate less creep strain than the homogeneous baseline.
The engineered multilayer coating will exhibit higher activation volumes than the homogeneous baseline.
The engineered multilayer coating will show more localized ordering at interfaces than the homogeneous baseline.
The proposed mechanism is primarily effective under compressive loading.
The proposed ordering mechanism is less effective under tensile loading because clustering continues to dominate.
The mechanism requires a temperature regime with enough atomic mobility for ordering.
The useful temperature regime must avoid bulk phase transformations or high-temperature disordering.
At sufficiently low temperatures, slow ordering kinetics will make the mechanism less effective.
Dislocations will accumulate or pile up near the engineered interfaces if those interfaces act as propagation barriers.
